Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Rohan's eyes still well up with tears when he recalls the day his granddaughter, Leela, was rushed to the hospital with a life-threatening illness. It's been two years since then, but the memory feels like it's happening right now, not something that's over. He can't quite piece together the events of that day into a coherent story, even for himself. Fragments keep surfacing - the sound of sirens, his daughter's frantic face, the antiseptic smell of the hospital - and they feel more real, more vivid than any ordinary memory. As a nanny, Rohan has always been devoted to Leela, but since her illness, he's become withdrawn, avoiding any situation that might remind him of that day. He won't seek medical help for his own ailments, fearing it will trigger another devastating diagnosis. He tries hard not to think about the trauma, keeping his mind occupied all the time with cooking, cleaning, or watching TV. But the memories seep in through the cracks - a child's cry on the street, a hospital drama on television - and he's instantly transported back to that terrible day. Rohan feels like he's lost himself in the process. The person he has become is unrecognisable to him - fearful, anxious, and uncertain. He distrusts others now, wondering if they're hiding something behind their smiles. His friends and family try to reassure him, but he can't shake off the feeling that people are not what they seem. Even his own daughter seems different, as if she's holding back some truth about Leela's health. Rohan is convinced that he has permanently changed for the worse. He feels like a part of him died in that hospital room, and he can't get it back. His relationships have suffered - he's become irritable, snapping at his daughter or Leela without reason. He's even started to question his own ability to care for Leela, feeling like he's not doing enough. At work, Rohan has become increasingly distant from the children in his care. He used to be the one who'd tell them stories and make them laugh, but now he just goes through the motions. His mind is always elsewhere - reliving that day, worrying about Leela's health, or fretting about some new catastrophe. The parents have started to notice the change, asking if everything is okay, but Rohan brushes it off, not wanting to burden them with his own troubles. Lately, Rohan's isolation has become too much to bear. His daughter sat him down last week and told him that Leela needs him - needs the old Rohan back. She gently suggested he seek help, and for the first time, Rohan felt a glimmer of hope. Maybe it's possible to reclaim himself, to find some way to make peace with what happened. He's terrified of facing his memories head-on, but more afraid of losing Leela and himself completely. With a deep breath, Rohan has finally agreed to seek help, hoping that somehow, someway, he can learn to live with the memories and find his way back to himself.
